explanations.answer: Drove them out with His hand
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The psalm says, “With Your hand You drove out the nations and planted our fathers there; You crushed the peoples and cast them out.” So God did the driving out AND the planting. That's a full day of work, and the fathers' only job was getting set down in the right spot, like a cookie on a tray.

explanations.answer: Made them friends of their fathers
explanations.explanation: That's a warm idea, friend, but it's not in this song. The psalm says God “crushed the peoples and cast them out.” Nobody's swapping recipes in that verse. It's God's hand clearing the land for their fathers.

explanations.answer: Let them share the land in peace
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, like everybody sharing one cooling rack. But the psalm says God drove out the nations and cast out the peoples. The fathers were planted there, and the nations weren't staying. So nobody's sharing in this story, friend.

Not this time, friend. The singers say the opposite: “…it was not by their sword that they took the land; their arm did not bring them victory.” It was by God's right hand, His arm and the light of His face. Plenty of folks would grab the credit, but these singers hand every bit of it to God.

That's right, it's false. The song says, “…it was not by their sword that they took the land; their arm did not bring them victory.” The credit goes to God's right hand, His arm and the light of His face. The singers don't hold onto any of it for themselves.
You got it, baker. The psalm ends that verse with “…because You favored them.” The reason is on God's side, not theirs. The singers don't list any other reason, so I won't make one up either.

Good guess, friend, but the song doesn't mention any asking. It says God did it “…because You favored them.” That's the only reason the singers give. I think it's worth noticing how little they put on their own side of the scale.

The psalm doesn't say that, friend. It never mentions laws in these verses. It says God gave the land “…because You favored them.” His favor is the reason, and the singers don't add a checklist to it.

That's it, baker. The psalmist says, “Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies.” Every win in that verse runs through God. This guy isn't counting on anything he could carry in his own hands.

That's what you'd expect, friend, but he says no to it. The psalmist says, “…I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me.” He's got a bow and a sword and he still doesn't lean on them. He says he's counting on God, and on God's name.

No walls or towers in this song, friend. The psalmist says, “Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies.” God and His name are what he's counting on. I'd call that a much sturdier thing to lean on than a pile of stones.

Right on the money, baker. They say God saves them from their enemies, and they sing, “In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever.” That's a confident song. The singers are looking at what God has done and cheering for Him.
Not at this point, friend. So far the singers aren't mourning anything. They're saying “You are my King, O God” and praising Him for saving them from their enemies. The sad notes haven't started yet.

There's no harvest in these verses, friend. The singers are talking about enemies, victories and the God who gives them. They say, “In God we have boasted all day long.” It's praise, but it's about God saving them, not about crops.

It goes the other way, friend. The singers say, “You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us.” Once God stops going out with their armies, they're the ones backing up. No winning streak in sight.

That's right, it's false. The psalm says, “You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us.” So they're the ones backing away. The song's mood has done a full turnaround.
That's the word, baker. The psalm says, “You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale.” Nothing changes hands. It's a hard line, and I think it's meant to sting.
Silver would at least be a payment, friend. The psalm says God sells His people “for nothing.” No coins come back in this sale at all. That's what makes the line so heavy.

Gold would be a big payday, friend, and this sale has no payday. The psalm says, “You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale.” The singers aren't naming a price. They're saying there isn't one.

Not even close, friend. The psalm says, “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us.” That's the neighbors looking down on them, not up at them. Respect isn't anywhere in that verse.

That's right, it's false. The psalm says, “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us.” The neighbors are mocking them. I think it hurts a lot more when it's the people living right next door.
Yes, baker. The psalmist says, “All day long my disgrace is before me.” Same “all day long” as the boasting, but now it's carrying shame. Same stretch of hours, very different song.

That was the earlier mood, friend. The psalmist says, “All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face.” The words “all day long” show up again, but this time they come with shame instead of boasting. The song has turned a corner.
No treasure here, friend. The psalmist says, “All day long my disgrace is before me.” Disgrace is what he sees, and it follows him around. It's about as far from a treasure chest as you can get.

The psalmist says the opposite, friend. He says, “All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant.” That “though” matters. They're saying they haven't forgotten God and haven't betrayed the covenant.

That's right, it's false. The psalmist says, “All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant.” That “though” is carrying a lot. The singers say they stayed faithful and the trouble came anyway.

That's it, baker. The psalmist says, “But You have crushed us in the lair of jackals; You have covered us with deepest darkness.” A lair of jackals is a rough place to be. And the darkness is covering them, not just brushing past.

Honor was the earlier story, friend. Now the psalmist says God has crushed them “in the lair of jackals” and covered them “with deepest darkness.” There's no honor handed out in that verse. It's a hard stretch.

The light of God's face did show up earlier in the song, friend, back in verse 3. In this verse the psalmist says God covered them “with deepest darkness.” Light and darkness are on opposite sides here. I think that's the point of the contrast.

Yes, baker. The psalmist says, “…would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart?” So if they'd forgotten God's name or reached out to a foreign god, God would have found out. The psalmist is saying they have nothing to hide.

It's true, friend. The psalmist asks, “…would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart?” If they'd forgotten God's name or spread out their hands to a foreign god, He would have known. Nothing in the heart is hidden from Him.
That's right, baker. The psalmist says, “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long.” The “Your” there is God. Whatever they're facing, they say it's on account of Him.

The fathers were in the opening of the song, friend, telling the old stories. But here the psalmist says, “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long.” The “Your” is God. So it's for God's sake, not their fathers'.
The neighbors only show up as mockers in this song, friend. The psalmist says, “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long.” That's God's sake. The singers don't say it's for anybody next door.

That's the cry, baker. He says, “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever.” He's loud, he's honest, and he's still talking to God. I think that's what faithfulness sounds like when it's hurting.

He doesn't ask that, friend. He says, “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise!” The psalmist already said God knows the secrets of the heart, and he never asks God to dig up anything. What he asks for is God to rise up.
No new king in this song, friend. Way back he said, “You are my King, O God.” So when trouble comes, he cries to the King he already has: “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise!”
Yes, baker. He asks, “Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?” He's not hiding the question. He puts it right in front of God.
It's true, friend. The psalmist asks, “Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?” He asks it straight to God's face, so to speak. Honest questions are allowed in this song.
That's the word, baker. The psalmist says, “For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth.” That's about as low as a person can get. I think you can hear them hugging the ground.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The psalmist says, “For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth.” They're sinking, not floating up. Down is where the whole verse is pointing.
There's no sea in this verse, friend. The psalmist says, “For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth.” Dust and earth are the words he picks. It's all ground level.

You got it, baker. The psalmist ends with, “Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion.” He's leaning on who God is, not on how they've done. That's a solid place to land when you're down in the dust.

They did say they stayed faithful, friend. But when he asks for rescue, he says, “Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion.” His ask rests on God's loving devotion. It doesn't rest on their record.

The fathers' stories opened the song, friend, but that's not what he points to here. He says, “Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion.” The last word goes to God's loving devotion. That's what the psalmist leans on.
